lesson.title: Different Roads, Same Destination: Convergent Evolution
lesson.summary: Convergent evolution occurs when unrelated lineages independently evolve similar traits because they face similar environmental or functional pressures, producing analogous structures rather than structures inherited from a shared ancestor.
lesson.body:
Convergent evolution is what happens when natural selection arrives at a similar solution more than once, in lineages that are not closely related and did not inherit the trait from a shared ancestor. This is the direct counterpart to the concept of analogous structures you have already encountered: analogous structures are the physical evidence, similar in function and often in outward form, but built from different underlying anatomy and arising through separate evolutionary histories. Convergent evolution is the process that produces that evidence.

The logic behind convergent evolution follows directly from natural selection acting on any population exposed to a particular environmental challenge or ecological role. If two unrelated lineages independently face a similar problem, moving efficiently through water, capturing flying insects in the dark, or surviving on a diet of hard seeds, natural selection tends to favor similar physical solutions in both, simply because there are only so many effective ways to solve a given physical or ecological problem. This connects back to adaptive radiation, where you saw a single lineage diversify into many different niches, convergent evolution is in some sense the mirror image, showing that when different lineages independently land in similar niches, they often end up looking surprisingly alike.

One of the clearest documented examples comes from comparing marsupial and placental mammals, two major mammal lineages that have been evolving separately since very early in mammalian history, largely isolated from each other because marsupials diversified mainly in Australia and South America while placentals diversified on the other continents. Despite this deep separation, strikingly similar body forms evolved independently on each side. The (now extinct) Tasmanian tiger, or thylacine, a marsupial predator, evolved a skull shape and overall body plan remarkably similar to that of placental wolves and dogs, despite the two groups sharing no recent common ancestor with that body plan. The marsupial sugar glider and the placental flying squirrel independently evolved a gliding membrane of skin stretched between their limbs, along with a broadly similar body shape, to solve the same problem of gliding between trees. Marsupial moles in Australia and placental moles elsewhere independently evolved powerful shovel-like forelimbs, reduced or vestigial eyes, and a streamlined, cylindrical body, all adaptations to a life spent tunneling underground. In every one of these pairs the resemblance is a product of similar selective pressures acting on different starting material, not shared ancestry.

Convergent evolution shows up just as clearly outside mammals. The camera-type eye, with a lens that focuses light onto a light sensitive retina, evolved independently in vertebrates and in cephalopods such as octopuses and squid, two groups whose most recent common ancestor almost certainly did not have anything resembling this kind of complex eye. Interestingly the two versions are wired differently, the vertebrate retina has its light sensing cells facing backward, with nerve fibers running in front of them, while the cephalopod retina has its light sensing cells facing forward, a difference that is itself evidence the two eyes were built independently rather than inherited from one ancestor. Streamlined, torpedo-shaped bodies with a dorsal fin are another repeated pattern, appearing independently in sharks (fish), dolphins (mammals), and the extinct ichthyosaurs (marine reptiles), three groups from three very different branches of the vertebrate family tree, all converging on a similar shape because it is an efficient solution to moving fast through water.

It is worth being explicit about why this matters for how biologists reconstruct evolutionary relationships, a theme that becomes central in the upcoming chapters on cladistics and phylogenetics. Because convergent traits are similar in appearance but not inherited from a common ancestor, they are considered misleading if used to group species by overall similarity. A classification system that grouped thylacines with wolves because they look alike, or dolphins with sharks because both are streamlined swimmers, would get the evolutionary relationships badly wrong. This is exactly why cladistics, which you are about to study, insists on using shared derived characters inherited from a common ancestor, rather than overall resemblance, to figure out which species are truly closely related.
